Australian Dollar Plunges to Record Low Amid Currency Turmoil, Sparking Economic Disruption

SYDNEY, June 14 – The Australian dollar tumbled to an all-time low against major currencies on Friday, deepening an ongoing currency crisis that has roiled financial markets and disrupted economic activity nationwide.

The dollar slid to 0.54 against the US dollar in early trading, its weakest level since the currency was floated in 1983. The plunge follows weeks of volatility and mounting concerns over Australia’s widening current account deficit, falling commodity prices, and a sharp outflow of foreign capital.

Traders cited a lack of confidence in the government’s fiscal position and uncertainty surrounding the Reserve Bank of Australia’s response as key drivers of the rout. The Reserve Bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 75 basis points on Thursday in an emergency move to stem the decline, but analysts say the action has so far failed to halt the slide.

“We are witnessing a classic currency crisis,” said Priya Malhotra, chief economist at the Australian Institute of Finance. “The rapid depreciation is pushing up import prices, igniting inflationary pressures, and undermining business and consumer confidence.”

Supermarkets across Sydney and Melbourne reported surging prices for imported goods, including electronics, medicines, and food staples such as rice and cooking oil. “We’ve had to raise prices on more than 400 imported products this week alone,” said Greg Latham, spokesperson for FoodMart, a national grocery chain. “Customers are frustrated, and we’re seeing a marked decrease in discretionary spending.”

Tourism operators and education providers, two major export sectors, said the weak dollar had led to a spike in foreign bookings and student enrollments, but the broader economy was suffering. Manufacturing Australia, an industry group, warned that soaring costs for imported machinery and raw materials were forcing smaller companies to cut production or lay off staff.

The Australian Council of Trade Unions reported a surge in calls from workers concerned about job security and falling real wages. “People are worried about making ends meet as household bills rise,” said ACTU President Sarah Hughes.

Prime Minister Daniel Evans called for calm, assuring the public that the government was “working closely with the Reserve Bank and international partners to restore stability.” The Treasury said it was considering additional fiscal measures to support vulnerable households and businesses if the currency turmoil persists.

Analysts warned that unless confidence returns soon, Australia risks deeper recessionary pressures, with rising unemployment and further declines in living standards.
